chunks: From him, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the jarri, the marmahi, the zimmir, and fish that have a shell/skin; is it forbidden?

He said to me, 'O Muhammad, recite this verse which is in Surah Al-An'am: "Say, I do not find within that was revealed to me [anything] forbidden to one who would eat it unless it be a dead animal or blood spilled out or the flesh of swine..."' (Note: The Imam quotes the core phrase regarding prohibition).

He said, so I recited it until I finished. Then he said, 'The forbidden is only that which Allah and His Messenger have forbidden in His Book. But they used to dislike certain things, so we dislike them too.'

key_terms.الزِّمِّيرِ: A type of fish, often identified as a mullet or similar species.
key_terms.الْجِرِّيِّ: A type of fish, often identified as a freshwater fish or carp-like species.
key_terms.الْمَارْمَاهِي: A type of fish, often identified as a sea bream or similar species.
key_terms.قِشْرٌ: Shell, skin, or crust, referring to the outer covering of the fish.
key_terms.يَعَافُونَ: They disliked or found repulsive (referring to the practice of the Imams/Companions regarding makruh items).

ai.seo_question: Are all types of fish halal in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the specific fish mentioned are not strictly *haram* by divine decree, as they are not explicitly named in the verse of Surah Al-An'am (6:145) which lists only three categories of forbidden meat. Instead, their status is *makruh* based on *istihbab* (preference) and the cultural practice of the Imams avoiding them, illustrating the Shia principle that not all disliked items are religiously prohibited. This distinction highlights the difference between *haram* (forbidden) and *makruh* (disliked but permissible), emphasizing that culinary aversion does not equate to legal prohibition.
